name: Tortoise ORM
summary: An async-native Python ORM with a Django-style API: models as classes, `await Model.filter(...)` queries, and built-in migrations since 1.0.
intro: Tortoise ORM was built for `asyncio` applications. You define models by subclassing `Model` and declaring fields, including `ForeignKeyField` and `ManyToManyField` relations, and every database call is awaited: `await Order.create(...)`, `await obj.save()`, `await Order.filter(amount__gt=100)`. Filters use Django’s double-underscore style (`name__icontains`, `customer__name`) and can follow relations into joins. Related objects aren’t loaded behind your back; you `await` them or load them up front with `fetch_related` and `prefetch_related`.

It runs on CPython 3.10 and later and talks to SQLite (`aiosqlite`), PostgreSQL (`asyncpg` or `psycopg`), MySQL and MariaDB (`asyncmy` or `aiomysql`), and Microsoft SQL Server and Oracle through `asyncodbc`. Version 1.0, released in February 2026, added a native migration framework (`tortoise makemigrations`, `tortoise migrate`, `tortoise sqlmigrate`) that replaces the separate Aerich tool, moved all ORM state into explicit `TortoiseContext` objects, and added PostgreSQL full-text search. Contrib modules register Tortoise in a FastAPI app’s lifespan and generate Pydantic models from Tortoise models with `pydantic_model_creator`.
strengths: Async from the ground up: every query is awaited, and a contrib module wires it into a FastAPI app’s lifespan
Familiar to Django users: model classes, `filter` and `exclude` with `field__lookup` arguments, and Django-like migration commands
Migrations are built in since 1.0, with autodetection, reversible operations, `RunPython` and `RunSQL`, and a command to preview the SQL
Small API surface for CRUD-heavy services: create, save, filter and prefetch without sessions to manage
limits: Async only: synchronous scripts or frameworks need an event loop around every call (`run_async` or `asyncio.run`)
Version 1.0 (February 2026) broke existing code: Python 3.10+, `use_tz` on by default, a new context-first architecture and removal of the old test helpers
A smaller ecosystem: about 5,600 GitHub stars against more than 12,000 for SQLAlchemy, which also does async through `AsyncSession` and supports external dialects
Its built-in migrations are new; projects started before 1.0 used Aerich, which the docs now call a legacy alternative

sections.title: Tortoise ORM and SQLAlchemy
sections.intro: SQLAlchemy has supported asyncio since version 1.4, so async alone is no longer a reason to pick Tortoise. The difference is the API style and how much each one covers.

rows.label: Style
values: Mapped classes used through a `Session`, plus Core for building SQL expressions

rows.label: Sync and async
values: Sync, plus `AsyncSession` and async engines since 1.4

rows.label: Loading relations
values: Eager loading, or `awaitable_attrs` under asyncio, where implicit lazy loading would fail

rows.label: Migrations
values: Alembic, a separate project from the SQLAlchemy authors

rows.label: Databases
values: SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle
The same five built in, plus external dialects

story: Andrey Bondar published Tortoise ORM in March 2018. The goal, as the README still puts it, was a lightweight, async-native object-relational mapper for Python “with a familiar Django-like API”. Nickolas Grigoriadis and Jinlong Peng have since made the most commits.

Version 0.16.0 in March 2020 added automatic Pydantic models built from Tortoise models. Migrations stayed outside the core: Aerich, a separate tool, was integrated into the install in October 2020. Tortoise 1.0 arrived in February 2026 after almost eight years of 0.x releases, with native migrations, explicit contexts in place of global state, and database schema support for PostgreSQL and SQL Server.

choices.why: The docs describe Tortoise as “inspired by Django”: model classes, querysets and double-underscore lookups such as `name__icontains` carry over, so the main new thing to learn is `await`.
Every database call returns an awaitable, so there is one code path, built for `asyncio` frameworks, instead of a sync API with async bolted on.
Loading a relation means a database round trip, which in async code has to be awaited. Tortoise makes that explicit with awaitable relations and `fetch_related`.

choices.choice: Migrations moved into the core in 1.0
choices.why: Migrations used to live in Aerich, a separate tool. The 1.0 framework autodetects model changes with `makemigrations` and `migrate` commands, and Aerich’s own README now sends 1.0 users to it.

timeline.text: Andrey Bondar releases Tortoise ORM 0.1.0 in March
0.16.0 in March builds Pydantic models from Tortoise models
Aerich migrations integrated into the install in October
Tortoise ORM 1.0 in February adds native migrations
